quotes.text: My overall plan is to provide 100,000 vacant lots facing gravel roads without utilities that will sell for about $50,000 a lot. With excellent off-grid appliances, catchment water tanks, solar heaters and septic systems, a minimum wage worker could afford to get a house and lot.
quotes.editor_note: Verbatim, two contiguous sentences from Fujiyama's written Civil Beat 2026 Q&A answering what steps he'd take on housing affordability — a campaign Q&A (text, not video-verifiable). States a bare-bones, off-grid state-land-lot approach aimed at minimum-wage affordability, a legible contrast with Cordery's fee-simple built-home approach on the same land-use axis. No edits.

quotes.text: Definitely, and I have a few other options as well. … Our whole real estate tax codes should be revisited especially for the agricultural zoned lands for owners with five acres and up to 300,000 acres.
quotes.editor_note: Verbatim from Fujiyama's written Civil Beat 2026 Q&A committing to protect the 2026 income tax cuts and naming a further tax-code change — a campaign Q&A (text, not video-verifiable). Cut one intervening sentence (a general aside about protecting lower-income residents that added no new position), marked with an ellipsis; both retained sentences are from the same continuous answer. States a cut-taxes-plus-revisit-agricultural-tax-code position.

quotes.text: Renewable energy at what costs? We should always allow for some other options. HELCO should never have a monopoly.
quotes.editor_note: Verbatim from Fujiyama's written Civil Beat 2026 Q&A responding to Hawai'i's LNG-bridge question, which engages the same fossil-fuels-role axis as the Compass question but frames it locally — a campaign Q&A (text, not video-verifiable). States an options-open, anti-monopoly position (resist a renewables-only mandate and break HELCO's market control so other energy sources can compete), paralleling Cordery's LNG-open/new-tech framing on the same axis via a market-structure mechanism instead. No edits.
